title: How God hides his face and the dragon is led
english: … or who give the body over to the stadium of martyrdom, or to the labours of the ascetic life, and in this way seem to destroy and kill themselves by being deprived of the enjoyments of life: “He who loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 10:39). For one who perishes in this way, according to the Saviour's word, and finds his life, the prayer and the blessing is a great thing. Anyone of sound mind would pray that it might come upon him, and would wisely say: “The blessing,” and so on (Job 29:13).

“I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame” (Job 29:15). As to the mind, he opened blind understandings and helped those maimed in soul, and he himself became their eye. To those lamed in the steps of the soul he gave feet; by his word he became their foot and led both by the hand. The eye stands for guidance of the understanding, the foot for guidance of conduct.

“I was a father of the powerless” (Job 29:16). These words show the voice of one who helps the powerless, the weak. “And a cause that I did not know, I searched out” (Job 29:16). You see his protection: it did not stop at money, nor at food and clothing; I stood forward even to the point of danger in another man's fight.

“And I broke the molars of the unjust” (Job 29:17). See how hard the thing was: he says that he set the matter right even when it had already been seized. Truly Christ, when he came, crushed the molars of the opposing powers. “The Lord has broken the molars of the lions” (Psalm 58:6), and it is written in the prophet: “From the midst of their teeth I snatched the prey” (Job 29:17).

“And I said: My age will grow old like the stem of a palm” (Job 29:18). See after how long a time he says this: not boasting or thinking great things of himself, but compelled to speak of God's providence, of the things in which he enjoyed it and of where he stands now.

“But now the least have laughed at me; now they admonish me in their turn, whose fathers I set at nought” (Job 30:1). Not that he made a practice of contempt, but that he knew them clearly, as the prophet said: “Every evildoer is set at nought before him” (Psalm 15:4). For he counted such people as nothing.
“And the strength of their hands, what is it to me? Over them the full end has perished. In want and famine he is barren, those who yesterday fled from waterless distress and misery” (Job 30:2-3).

From Olympiodorus and Origen: I did not even ask them for any help, he says, that they should use such words against me on that account. They had long owed a penalty, being wicked, and in a way the punishment flew away from them. Or else: they longed for death because of their extreme poverty and did not obtain it, and not even their want brought them to their senses so as to become begetters of good; they remained barren, those who only yesterday, a little while ago, had escaped from the desert and their misfortunes. He seems to disparage them as low-born, from obscure villages and poor fathers. “Over them the full end has perished”: that is, they never brought anything good to completion.

“Those who go round the mallows on an echoing place, whose food was mallows” (Job 30:4). Mallow is a plant, they say, that quickly fills the one who eats it. “On an echoing place”: that is, on ravines and rocky ground, for such places ring and give back the voices of those who speak. Or he calls echoing the wooded place where the breath of the winds stirs the trees and makes a sound. So he says that these men roamed the woods and the ravines and the places where running waters sound and babble; in their great want they searched out plants and scraped the roots of trees for food, as some comfort in their hunger.
“Dishonoured and despised, in want of every good thing” (Job 30:4). It is another wickedness to be like this even in poverty.
“For would that I could lay hands on myself” (Job 30:24). You see that he says “if I could” not because of weakness but because he was forbidden.
“And I have stood in the assembly crying out” (Job 30:28). Because of the excess of his sufferings he is not ashamed even of the crowd of the gathering.

“I have become a brother of sirens and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30:29). I have fallen, he says, into the wildness of the birds; I have forgotten my own nature, and I am in no better state than they.

“For I have stood in a just balance, and the Lord knows my innocence, if my foot has turned aside from the way …” (Job 31:6-7). What exactness! No one could say that I misused my former wealth and goods for idleness and dissipation and so pay this penalty and have been changed, God having laid on me a fitting medicine. For to the one who loves laughter and play and is given to luxury he fittingly sets the opposite …

The old English printed the catena's verse numerals as '[[quote >> ...]]' links to wrong or non-existent verses (Job 2:3, 5:18, 6:16, 9:22, 26:7, 28:16, 33:11, 40:1, 40:4, 44:18), misquoted 'From the midst of their teeth I snatched the prey' as Job 5:18, and left the catena heading '(Olympiodorus, Origen)' floating inside a paragraph. Lemmas now carry the catena's own verse numbers (Job 29:13-31:7). The heading Ὀλυμπιοδώρου, Ὠριγένους is printed as the catena gives it, as a lead-in to the note it heads ('From Olympiodorus and Origen:'); the catena gives no mark where that joint attribution ends, so none is invented. 'καθὰ πόθεν' (29:17 note) is corrupt; rendered by sense. φιλοπταίσμονα read as φιλοπαίγμονα ('play').

title: Lament, justice, and the measure of affliction
english: He will be placed in ruin, handed over to mourning and many-lamenting in life; yet he, fleeing from crowds and pursuing men who play and make merry, what kind of words would he fall into, a life of shame and darkness? Since I had been exhausted and broken, I did not descend into the evils of that life. F my sorrowful women often said: Who would satisfy us with his   flesh, so very useful to me? Instead of enjoying his life, for I was sweet to them. Lb. A stranger was not turned away outside, and my door was open   to all who came. For he did not merely receive them by hosting, but also provided for the poverty that followed. Ch. 24, 1. And Job ceased speaking. Job was silent, giving them words to speak; yet he looked up and called God as witness, declaring that his friends had ceased to accuse. 14. For I will speak, while you listen, until you are wearied by words, and until I understand you. Perhaps he means that even when you should have rebuked, as was right, you did not rebuke; or that later you fell silent. Thus: For I will speak, while you listen. Ch. 25, 12. How can you say: I am righteous, and he did not listen to me? What then happened? Did he not think this: Elihu indeed took this, but Job did not say with such an opinion, that this one is more righteous than God; but that these things happened to him, and he did not accuse God of injustice. And Elihu took this; but he rightly accused those who gave to God a portion and denied Him. 381 k. I will speak, to rest by opening my lips. The one who is a thoughtful listener, full of words, speaks and rests, as if emptying and casting off his abundance, saying: I will speak to rest. Ch. 26, 18. He who is not ashamed before an honorable person, nor knows how to grant honor to the simple. For even if you do not know, you must yield much to him and his glory, so as not to seek all things, but to learn. 23. That he will no longer set against a man. It seems he says this: now the good and the bad lie within us, but in the coming age, not anymore. 10. That toward the strong the one says: If I take, I will not hold back, without myself I will see; show me. Some interpreted this as: no one dares to say to the stronger that you unjustly took my things, not for reproach, but against my will; show that you acted rightly. If no one dares speak to the powerful, how dare you speak against God? And the Ally explained: we undertook an oath toward God, not outside release, clarify for me. And he understood: because we undertook the oath concerning God, Elius says, I do not hold back, but proceed freely. If I speak wrongly, clarify, instead of examining the word. –I think this is how the text is meant: not because I chose to speak concerning God, but you must agree simply, as I demand; without myself I will see, show me, instead of: apart from my words I want to know if you can oppose, so you may say I offer peace and grasp the word if you can. Ch. 45, 5. Look up to heaven. No lover of the world looks up to heaven; let us not love the world or its things. If we love these, we do not look to heaven. If you sinned, what will you do? That is, you will not wrong him, nor benefit, being righteous; for indeed... If I sinned, what can I do? what will I do, he says; this to say: For what reason? does one care about his sinning if not wronged? not as a harm endured? X. The one appointing nocturnal guards. Do you wish to see how God appoints nocturnal guards? The whole age is night, darkness. The light is kept for you; what you see now as light, you see through a mirror. And: In your light we shall see light; we intend to see it. Is not the age all night? since it is night, enemies abound, many beasts roam. Since night is the time of life's darkness, guards must be appointed for this night, so the guards, those over the nights, may guard those in night and come to guard us from robbers. Who then are the guards, appointed by God in these nocturnal watches? The Lord's angel interposes around those who fear Him, and rescues them; these are the angels who in night...

title: Foundations, measure, and the end of the wicked
english: They stand as our guardians. (Ch. 40, 5) If you have any knowledge, tell me: who established the earth's dimensions? Or who applied the measuring rod to it? Some have attempted to offer a secular explanation regarding the earth's scale, claiming its diameter spans twenty-five myriads of stadia. Yet the Word reveals that the earth's true measure remains beyond all human comprehension; only the Savior, who is also the Creator, possesses this knowledge. He spoke of 'measures' in the plural rather than a single 'measure' to illustrate the diverse variations found across the earth. Tell me, what could be the measure of that which carries the fragrances of the East? What is the measure of that which carries the spices or the living creatures? Since not all things are found in every place, these dimensions are determined by the Word of God. The earth has not simply reached this size by chance or through random occurrence. It seems to me that even if accidental elements were included, they would be out of place; conversely, if they were removed, the entire structure would be ruined according to the divine logic. The mention of measures and the rod alludes to this.

Who is it that has laid the cornerstone upon the earth? Who has set this cornerstone so that the world stands so firmly, as if built upon a secure and established foundation? It is by the counsel of God, for all the boundaries of the earth are held in His hand. This cornerstone can be understood as a reference to the Only-begotten Son of God, who became flesh through us, as the Psalms declare: [[quote >> Bible:Psalms 118:22 >> A stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone]]. Having descended to earth through the Father's favor, He united the two peoples—both Jew and Gentile—just as a cornerstone binds two walls together. (14) I said to her, 'It shall flow up to this point and will not overflow.' The Ally replied, 'Let the limit of your waves be so commanded.' For the water is held securely as if by iron bars, yet it moves with ease as if following a set order. I argued, and it cannot be disputed, that this occurs without any external force pushing it, even while it is being lashed by great power and strength. He did not allow the waters to be calm or tranquil so that they might proclaim God's power, struggling against the laws of nature by His command and conquering all through His decree. Had the water been peaceful, many would have attributed its order to the natural properties of water; but now, being tossed, scourged, and driven inward, yet unable to breach its boundaries, it proclaims the might of God through its very turbulence. (Ch. 28, 27) What provided food for the raven? It is said that they do not nurture their young, yet the adults, being large, do provide sustenance in their own way. But who truly nourishes the offspring? Is it not the Word of God? As the Gospel states: [[quote >> Bible:Matthew 6:26 >> Look at the birds of the air; they do not sow or reap, yet your heavenly Father feeds them]]. (Ch. 28, 27) By whose command is the eagle lifted high? And how does the vulture, having settled upon a carcass, cry out from a high rock in secret? ...If there is any rational wisdom in carnivores, it is found in the natural knowledge present in each, directed toward the knowledge of the one I call the dead, even as one carries a vulture. (Ch. 24) Why am I still being judged, being admonished and rebuked by the Lord while I am nothing? Why does he ask why he is being judged for his future? From the beginning, he withdrew from primary things. He says he is defeated by you in matters of justice; why do you advance your judgment so boldly? For what answer is possible? How can one face such a master? He says he was continuing to seek the cause of the plague that befell him, but he summoned no one regarding the creation, and he has nothing to say in response to what has been spoken. —He departs, as if not even rebuking the Lord, being admonished, the wretched man. (Ch. 4, 4) To live as a man by your strength—I will ask you, and you shall answer me. For those who hold rights and do not flee from adversaries, victory comes through their possession. He then defends himself, claiming that men do not concern him; it is clear from that context why this temptation came upon you. I grant you boldness: I will ask, and you shall answer. (Ch. 3) He believes I have used you for any purpose other than to demonstrate your justice. He says the present matter is for profit; he claims he does not speak to condemn, but to prove him just. Or, regarding the temptation, he calls forgiveness a profit, suggesting he was commanded to do this so that he might become something else; he did not say it was so he might change, but so that you might reveal what you truly are and instruct others. See then: he did not say he might become just (for which justice is required...)
